Instructive

/in-STRUK-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Instructive means serving to teach, inform, or provide useful insight.

The failed launch proved more instructive than a dozen successes, exposing three design flaws in one afternoon.

Worked Example

The museum's most popular exhibit is a wall of broken pots. Each shard is labeled with what went wrong: fired too fast, glazed too thick, cooled unevenly. Visiting potters linger there longer than at the flawless masterpieces two rooms over. 'The perfect pieces are beautiful,' the curator explains, 'but the broken ones are instructive — every crack teaches you something you can use tomorrow.'

Each labeled crack teaches a usable lesson — the broken pots serve to inform and improve the visitor's own craft, which is exactly what instructive means.

How Instructive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

educational

educational: providing knowledge or training

illuminating

illuminating: shedding light that aids understanding

Antonyms

misleading

misleading: creating a false impression

confusing

confusing: muddling rather than clarifying

How Strong Is It? — informative → instructive → revelatory

informative vs. instructive

informative vs. instructive: Informative is weaker than instructive: informative material supplies facts, while instructive material teaches you something you can actually use.

revelatory vs. instructive

revelatory vs. instructive: Revelatory is stronger than instructive — a revelatory experience transforms how you see the whole subject, while an instructive one adds a solid, usable lesson.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of instructive.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: on; upon

Root — struct

Root — struct: to build (Latin struere, structus)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to; having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Instructive assembles just as the unit teaches: in- ('on, upon') + struct ('to build' — the root of structure and infrastructure) + -ive ('tending to'). To instruct is literally to 'build knowledge onto' someone, layer by layer, and instructive means 'characterized by that building' — an instructive failure adds a course of bricks to what you know.

Use the root in a new word: infrastructure

Use the root in a new word: infrastructure: Roads and power grids are infrastructure, 'built beneath' everything else — struere, 'to build,' the same root that lets an instructive example build up your understanding.
